title: GOD NEVER COMMANDED YOU TO STAY AND BE DESTROYED: THE TERRIFYING TRUTH ABOUT ABUSIVE PASTORS AND SPIRITUAL AUTHORITY
paragraphs: GOD NEVER COMMANDED YOU TO STAY AND BE DESTROYED: THE TERRIFYING TRUTH ABOUT ABUSIVE PASTORS AND SPIRITUAL AUTHORITY
When the person who was supposed to shepherd your soul becomes the reason you're afraid of God, leaving may not be rebellion. It may be the moment you finally understand whom you truly belong to.
There is a kind of pain that doesn't come from the world.
It comes from the pulpit.
It comes from the mouth of someone who once prayed over you, baptized your children, visited your family, and told you that God had placed him in your life to protect your soul.
Someone you trusted.
Someone you defended.
Someone you believed was speaking for God.
And then, one day, you began noticing something that didn't feel right.
Questions were treated like rebellion.
Disagreement was called pride.
Boundaries were labeled dishonor.
Your private struggles became weapons against you.
Your loyalty was constantly tested, but the pastor's conduct was never allowed to be questioned.
And whenever you tried to explain how deeply you were hurting, the same Scripture was brought out like a hammer.
"Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves..." (Hebrews 13:17, KJV).
So you stayed.
Not because you were at peace.
Not because everything was right.
But because you were terrified that leaving your pastor might mean leaving God.
Perhaps you've whispered this question in the darkness, afraid even to say it aloud:
"Lord, if I walk away from this pastor, am I walking away from You?"
What if the answer you've been afraid to hear is the very truth that could begin setting you free?
What if the Bible never gave a pastor permission to become your master?
And what if the Jesus who commands His shepherds to care for the flock also holds them accountable when they wound it?
Before we go any further, understand something.
This is not an attack on faithful pastors.
There are humble, courageous, sacrificial shepherds who preach Christ faithfully, serve when nobody is watching, receive correction, and genuinely love the people entrusted to their care.
They deserve our prayers, encouragement, and appropriate respect.
But protecting faithful pastors must never require protecting abusive ones.
And honoring biblical authority must never require surrendering the authority of Jesus Christ.
Because the moment a spiritual leader begins demanding the kind of unquestioning allegiance that belongs to Christ alone, something has gone terribly wrong.
And Scripture has much more to say about that than many wounded believers have ever been allowed to hear.
Let's begin with the verse that has kept countless frightened Christians silent.
Hebrews 13:17.
In the King James Version, it reads:
"Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account..."
Now consider the Greek text behind the opening command:
Πείθεσθε τοῖς ἡγουμένοις ὑμῶν
Peithesthe tois hēgoumenois hymōn.
The verb peithesthe comes from peithō, a word associated with persuasion, trust, and being convinced. In this grammatical form and context, it carries the sense of heeding or obeying one's leaders.
This does not erase the real biblical responsibility to respond respectfully to faithful spiritual leadership.
But it does challenge the idea that the verse establishes an unlimited right to command.
The passage does not say pastors are infallible.
It does not say their instructions override Scripture.
It does not say every disagreement is sinful.
And it certainly does not say a believer must endure intimidation, exploitation, assault, or coercive control to prove loyalty to God.
Read the reason Hebrews gives for honoring spiritual leaders.
They "watch for your souls, as they that must give account."
Account.
That word should make every pastor tremble.
Spiritual authority is not a throne from which a leader escapes scrutiny.
It is a stewardship for which that leader must answer before God.
A pastor is not given authority so he can protect his reputation at the expense of your well-being.
He is entrusted with responsibility to care for people who belong to someone else.
Jesus.
And that distinction changes everything.
Because sheep do not belong to the shepherd who serves them.
They belong to the Chief Shepherd.
Peter makes this unmistakably clear.
In 1 Peter 5:2–3, church elders are instructed to shepherd God's flock willingly, not for dishonest gain, and not by dominating those entrusted to them.
The Greek expression is devastatingly relevant:
μηδ᾽ ὡς κατακυριεύοντες τῶν κλήρων
Mēd' hōs katakyrieuontes tōn klērōn.
The verb katakyrieuō communicates the idea of exercising mastery or domineering over others.
Peter is not merely encouraging pastors to be nicer.
He is forbidding a form of leadership that seeks to dominate God's people.
And this command comes from a man who knew what it meant to be corrected by Jesus Himself.
Peter had once been so confident in his own loyalty that he insisted he would never deny Christ.
Then, in a courtyard, under pressure, he denied Him three times.
He knew what failure looked like.
He knew what restoration felt like.
And when the risen Jesus restored Peter in John 21, the repeated commission was not, "Make My sheep obey you."
It was:
"Feed my lambs."
"Feed my sheep."
The flock remained Christ's.
Not Peter's.
Not the apostles'.
Not any pastor's today.
A shepherd who treats God's people as personal property has forgotten whose name is written over the flock.
And perhaps this is where your heart begins to ache.
Because you remember when you genuinely loved your church.
You weren't looking for trouble.
You weren't trying to divide anyone.
You were the person who arrived early.
Who cleaned the chairs.
Who gave when money was tight.
Who prayed for the pastor's family.
Who defended the ministry when others criticized it.
You overlooked harsh words because you thought the pastor was simply tired.
You excused humiliation because you thought perhaps God was correcting your pride.
You stayed quiet when something seemed wrong because you didn't want to be accused of dishonoring the Lord.
Until one day, you realized you were no longer serving from love.
You were serving from fear.
Fear of being publicly shamed.
Fear of losing your friends.
Fear of being called rebellious.
Fear that God would punish you if you walked away.
And maybe the most heartbreaking part was this:
You still loved Jesus.
You just didn't know how to separate His voice from the voice of someone who claimed to represent Him.
If that's where you are, please hear what Scripture actually says.
In Ezekiel 34, God confronts the shepherds of Israel who used their position for themselves while neglecting those entrusted to them.
The Lord declares:
"Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?" (Ezekiel 34:2, KJV).
Then comes an indictment that should shake every abusive spiritual leader.
"The diseased have ye not strengthened, neither have ye healed that which was sick, neither have ye bound up that which was broken..." (Ezekiel 34:4, KJV).
And the verse continues:
"...but with force and with cruelty have ye ruled them."
The Hebrew text uses the words:
בְּחָזְקָה וּבְפָרֶךְ
Beḥozqāh uvefārek.
These expressions convey ruling with force and harshness.
God was not impressed by the shepherds' titles.
He was not persuaded by their religious positions.
He saw how they treated His people.
And He condemned it.
Read that again.
God condemned the leaders who ruled His flock through harshness.
He did not tell the wounded sheep that their suffering was proof of their faithfulness.
He did not accuse them of rebellion for being scattered by cruel leadership.
Instead, He promised to intervene.
In Ezekiel 34:10, God declares that He will require His flock at the shepherds' hands and cause them to cease feeding the flock.
And in verse 16, He promises:
"I will seek that which was lost, and bring again that which was driven away, and will bind up that which was broken..."
Do you see the heart of God?
He does not celebrate the destruction of His sheep.
He seeks them.
He gathers them.
He binds their wounds.
He holds unfaithful shepherds accountable.
The original context concerns Israel's corrupt shepherds and God's promised restoration of His people. We should not pretend every detail is a direct instruction about modern church membership.
But the moral revelation is unmistakable.
God opposes leaders who exploit those they were called to protect.
And His concern for the wounded has not disappeared.
Now consider something even more startling.
Jesus Himself confronted religious authorities who used spiritual status to burden others.
In Matthew 23:4, He said:
"For they bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne, and lay them on men's shoulders; but they themselves will not move them with one of their fingers."
These were religious leaders.
People who knew Scripture.
People who appeared respectable.
People who could speak eloquently about holiness while failing to practice mercy, justice, and faithfulness.
Jesus did not confuse religious influence with spiritual integrity.
He exposed hypocrisy.
He confronted manipulation.
He warned against leadership that loved titles, recognition, and power.
And in Matthew 20:25–28, He contrasted the rulers who exercised dominion over others with the kind of leadership expected among His disciples.
"Whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister."
The Greek word translated "minister" is διάκονος (diakonos), meaning servant or one who ministers.
Jesus overturned the world's definition of greatness.
In His kingdom, leadership is not permission to crush people beneath you.
It is a calling to serve them.
And Jesus did not merely preach that truth.
He demonstrated it.
The King of glory knelt and washed His disciples' feet.
The One who possessed all authority did not use that authority to satisfy selfish ambition.
He humbled Himself.
He loved.
He served.
And ultimately, He gave His life for His people.

Now place that picture beside the behavior of a pastor who threatens people for questioning financial decisions, humiliates members who disagree, demands secrecy about misconduct, or uses spiritual fear to maintain control.
Do those pictures look alike?
Not every stern correction is abuse.
Not every uncomfortable sermon is manipulation.
Not every church disagreement proves that a pastor is corrupt.
Biblical leaders sometimes must confront genuine sin, teach difficult truths, and exercise appropriate church discipline.
But correction is not the same as cruelty.
Accountability is not the same as intimidation.
Church discipline is not permission to bypass truth, fairness, and love.
And pastoral authority is not a license to threaten someone's safety, livelihood, family, or relationship with God.
A faithful pastor may challenge your behavior.
An abusive pastor may try to control your conscience.
A faithful pastor points you toward Scripture.
An abusive pastor may twist Scripture to make himself impossible to question.
A faithful pastor welcomes appropriate accountability.
An abusive pastor may insist that accountability itself is rebellion.
The difference matters.
Especially when someone tells you that you must remain under abusive authority because Romans 13 commands submission.
Romans 13 primarily addresses governing authorities, not a pastor's unrestricted control over a congregation.
And even earthly authority is never absolute.
When the apostles were commanded to stop speaking in Jesus' name, Peter and the other apostles answered:
"We ought to obey God rather than men." (Acts 5:29, KJV).
The Greek is direct:
Πειθαρχεῖν δεῖ θεῷ μᾶλλον ἢ ἀνθρώποις.
Peitharchein dei theō mallon ē anthrōpois.
It is necessary to obey God rather than human beings.
This passage concerns the apostles' obedience to God's commission in the face of opposition from human authorities. It is not a blanket excuse to reject every leader we dislike.
But it establishes a vital principle.
Human authority cannot rightfully demand disobedience to God.
And no pastor can claim a higher allegiance than the Lord Jesus Christ.
Now perhaps someone has warned you:
"Touch not mine anointed."
Those words come from passages such as Psalm 105:15 and 1 Chronicles 16:22.
In their original setting, they concern God's protection of His people, particularly the patriarchs, against those who would harm them.
They do not establish a special exemption from investigation or correction for modern pastors.
Scripture itself demonstrates that spiritual leaders can be confronted.
In Galatians 2:11–14, Paul publicly opposed Peter when Peter's conduct contradicted the truth of the Gospel.
Imagine that.
Peter.
An apostle.
A man personally commissioned by the risen Christ.
Yet his behavior was not beyond correction.
And in 1 Timothy 5:19–20, Paul gives instructions concerning accusations against elders, requiring proper witnesses and addressing those who persist in sin.
The passage protects leaders against careless accusations while also refusing to place them beyond accountability.
Both truths matter.
False accusations can destroy innocent people.
But suppressing credible accusations can allow real harm to continue.
Biblical justice requires neither gullibility nor a cover-up.
It requires truth.
Evidence.
Fairness.
Courage.
And concern for those who may be in danger.

If a pastor is physically or sexually abusive, threatens violence, exploits children, or commits other serious wrongdoing, protecting the vulnerable must take priority over protecting an institution's reputation.
Contact appropriate civil authorities or emergency services when necessary. Seek independent professional help and a safe place if you are in danger.
Do not assume that a private church meeting is an adequate substitute for reporting suspected crimes.
And do not allow anyone to use the language of forgiveness to pressure you into silence.
Forgiveness does not mean pretending evil never happened.
Repentance is not merely saying, "I'm sorry you were offended."
Restoration to ministry is not automatic.
Reconciliation requires more than one person's willingness.
And trust cannot be demanded simply because someone carries a religious title.
A pastor may be forgiven by God and still face legal consequences, removal from leadership, and lasting restrictions necessary to protect others.
Grace does not erase accountability.
The cross is not a hiding place for unrepentant abuse.
It is where sin is exposed in all its seriousness and where mercy is offered through the sacrifice of Jesus Christ.
And that brings us to one of the most painful questions in this entire conversation.
Does leaving an abusive pastor mean abandoning the church?
No.
Not necessarily.
A particular congregation is not the entire body of Christ.
A pastor is not the Savior.
And remaining under one leader's authority is not the definition of faithfulness to Jesus.
Hebrews 10:24–25 encourages believers to gather, encourage one another, and persevere in fellowship.
That remains important.
But the command to pursue Christian fellowship is not a command to remain indefinitely in a harmful congregation.
You can leave an abusive environment while continuing to love Christ, seek healthy fellowship, and remain committed to His people.
Sometimes that journey is complicated.
You may need time to recover.
You may struggle to trust another pastor.
You may feel anxious when you hear a sermon about obedience.
A familiar worship song may bring back memories you wish you could forget.
You might even open your Bible and feel your stomach tighten because certain verses were repeatedly used to frighten you.
That doesn't mean Scripture itself was your enemy.
It may mean someone used sacred words in a way that deeply wounded you.
And healing may involve slowly rediscovering what those passages actually say.
With patient, trustworthy people.
Without pressure.
Without threats.
Without being forced to pretend you're healed before you are.
There is a beautiful moment in John 9 that speaks to people who have been rejected by religious authorities.
Jesus heals a man who had been blind.
But the religious leaders interrogate him, challenge his testimony, and eventually cast him out.
Then John 9:35 tells us something extraordinary.
"Jesus heard that they had cast him out; and when he had found him..."
Stop there.
"When he had found him."
The man had been rejected by religious authorities.
But Jesus went looking for him.
The passage is primarily about Jesus revealing Himself as the Son of Man and bringing spiritual sight to one who believed, while exposing the blindness of those who rejected Him.
It is not specifically a manual for leaving an abusive church.
Yet the scene reveals something deeply comforting about Christ's character.
Being rejected by religious leaders did not mean being rejected by Jesus.
The man lost acceptance within a religious community.
But he encountered the One worthy of his worship.
And when Jesus revealed Himself, the man responded:
"Lord, I believe." (John 9:38, KJV).
Then he worshiped Him.
Not the institution that expelled him.
Not the leaders who interrogated him.
Jesus.
Perhaps that is the distinction your heart has been struggling to make.
You were taught to associate one pastor's approval with God's approval.
One congregation's acceptance with your spiritual security.
One leader's anger with divine judgment.
But the Gospel tells a different story.
Your standing before God does not rest on a pastor's personal opinion of you.
It rests on Jesus Christ.
The One who lived without sin.
The One who willingly went to the cross.
The One who bore sin and conquered death.
The One who calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness through faith in Him.
And the One who remains the Head of His Church.
Colossians 1:18 says:
"And he is the head of the body, the church..."
He.
Not your pastor.
Not a bishop.
Not a denomination.
Not the founder of a ministry.
Jesus Christ.
The Church belongs to Him.
And every legitimate spiritual leader serves beneath His authority.
Now I want to speak to the person who has been carrying guilt for leaving.
Maybe you walked away months ago.
Maybe years.
But sometimes you still hear the pastor's warning in your mind.
"God will remove His blessing from your life."
"You'll never prosper outside this covering."
"Anyone who leaves this ministry is walking away from God's will."
And every time something painful happens, you wonder whether the threat was true.
Your finances became difficult.
Your marriage went through a struggle.
You lost a job.
Someone you love became sick.
And suddenly you began connecting every hardship to the day you left that church.
But listen carefully.
The Bible does not teach that leaving an abusive pastor automatically brings a curse upon your life.
Jesus Himself told His disciples that they would experience trouble in this world (John 16:33).
Hardship is not proof that an abusive leader's threats were prophetic.
Suffering is not automatically divine punishment.
And a pastor's displeasure does not determine your eternal standing before God.
Romans 8:1 declares:
"There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus..."
The assurance belongs to those who are in Christ.
Not those who remain loyal to a particular personality.
Not those who never question a ministry.
Not those who endure mistreatment to earn approval.
Those who are in Christ Jesus.
This does not mean Christians are free from correction or that every decision we make is right.
It means our hope is anchored in Christ's saving work, not in the control of another human being.
And if you've been wounded by someone who preached grace while practicing cruelty, I want you to understand one more thing.
You do not have to call evil good in order to be forgiving.
You do not have to deny what happened to demonstrate spiritual maturity.
You do not have to return to an unsafe environment to prove that you have a Christlike heart.
You can pray for someone's repentance while maintaining firm boundaries.
You can refuse revenge while pursuing justice.
You can forgive without immediately restoring trust.
You can honor the biblical office of a pastor without excusing the sins of a person occupying that office.
And you can acknowledge your own imperfections without accepting responsibility for another person's abusive choices.
That is not hatred.
That is moral clarity.
And sometimes moral clarity is where healing begins.
But perhaps you are not the person who was abused.
Perhaps you are a pastor reading this.
A ministry leader.
An elder.
A teacher.
Someone entrusted with souls.
Then hear this with the seriousness it deserves.
Your people are not your possessions.
Their money is not your entitlement.
Their silence is not proof of unity.
Their fear is not evidence of spiritual maturity.
And their inability to challenge you is not necessarily a sign that God has established your authority.
A congregation can appear orderly while its members are terrified.
A ministry can grow numerically while people are being wounded privately.
A leader can preach powerful sermons and still need to repent of serious wrongdoing.
Jesus warned in Matthew 7:22–23 that impressive religious activity is not, by itself, proof of a genuine relationship with Him.
Spiritual gifts are not substitutes for godly character.
Public influence is not immunity from judgment.
And success is not the same as faithfulness.
If you have harmed people, repentance requires more than an emotional apology from the pulpit.
It means telling the truth.
Ceasing harmful behavior.
Accepting appropriate accountability.
Making restitution where possible.
Cooperating with legitimate investigations.
And relinquishing authority when necessary.
It means caring more about the people you hurt than about preserving the image you built.
Because the Church does not need another untouchable personality.
It needs shepherds who resemble Jesus.
And to the faithful pastors who have quietly served through exhaustion, criticism, sacrifice, and tears, please do not hear this as an accusation against you.
Your work matters.
Your integrity matters.
Your willingness to be accountable matters.
And one of the greatest ways to honor your calling is to help make the Church a place where truth can be spoken without fear.
Where vulnerable people are protected.
Where accusations are handled fairly.
Where repentance is real.
Where Christ is greater than the reputation of any leader.
That kind of shepherding is worthy of respect.
Now return with me to the person sitting alone after leaving a harmful church.
Maybe you're still holding your Bible.
Maybe you haven't opened it in weeks.
Maybe you miss the people.
The music.
The fellowship.
The feeling of belonging somewhere.
Maybe part of you wishes you could go back to the days before you discovered what was happening.
Because losing trust in a spiritual leader can feel like losing an entire world.
And nobody tells you how lonely that can be.
Nobody prepares you for the friends who stop calling.
For the messages that go unanswered.
For the rumors.
For the people who say, "There are two sides to every story," without ever asking whether you're safe.
For the ache of realizing that some people are more concerned about the ministry's reputation than the wounds of the people who attended it.
But please don't let the failures of people who claimed to represent Christ become the final word about Christ Himself.
Look at Him again.
Look at the Jesus who welcomed the weary.
The Jesus who confronted hypocrisy.
The Jesus who defended the dignity of those society despised.
The Jesus who told His disciples not to imitate rulers who lorded authority over others.
The Jesus who laid down His life for the sheep.
In John 10:11, He said:
"I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep."
The Greek expression is:
ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός
Ho poimēn ho kalos.
"The good shepherd."
The word kalos carries the sense of good, noble, or excellent.
Jesus is not merely a shepherd with a religious title.
He is the true and noble Shepherd whose character reveals what faithful shepherding should be.
He does not exploit the sheep for His own comfort.
He gives Himself for them.
And this is where the Gospel becomes more than a religious idea.
Because every one of us needs more than escape from bad leadership.
We need redemption from sin.
We need forgiveness.
We need a Savior.
Even the deepest wounds inflicted by others do not remove our own need for God's grace.
And the astonishing news of Christianity is that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
He bore our sins in His body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24).
He died and rose again.
He calls us to turn from sin and trust in Him.
He offers forgiveness that cannot be purchased through offerings, earned through ministry service, or secured by pleasing a human leader.
And through Him, wounded people can begin discovering that their story is not finished.
Not every scar disappears quickly.
Not every relationship can be restored.
Not every injustice receives full resolution in this life.
But the resurrection of Jesus declares that evil, sin, and death will not have the final word.
And the Lord who will ultimately judge with perfect righteousness is also the Savior who welcomes those who come to Him.
Maybe your story has been marked by scandal.
The scandal of betrayal.
The scandal of hypocrisy.
The scandal of discovering that someone who spoke about holiness was secretly doing harm.
But scandal does not have to become the final chapter.
Because Jesus still redeems.
Jesus still restores.
Jesus still calls people out of darkness.
And Jesus still writes stories that human failure could never have imagined.
Not because the scandal was harmless.
Not because justice no longer matters.
Not because the past can simply be erased.
But because the grace of Christ is greater than the power of sin to define the future of those who belong to Him.
And perhaps today, the first step toward that grace is simply telling the truth.
"I was hurt."
"I was afraid."
"I confused a pastor's voice with God's voice."
"I still believe in Jesus, but I need help learning to trust again."
Or maybe:
"Lord, I have been using my position to control people. Forgive me. Teach me to repent."
If any of those words describe where you are, you are not required to reveal private details publicly.
You don't need to explain everything.
Sometimes a few honest words are enough to remind another wounded believer that they are not alone.
And if this article has exposed something in your own leadership, let your response be more than a comment.
Let it become repentance expressed through real change.
I also want to ask you to think of someone who may desperately need to read this.
A friend who stopped attending church and never explained why.
A family member who has been told that questioning a pastor is rebellion.
A young believer who thinks obedience to God means tolerating mistreatment.
A ministry worker who is exhausted from trying to earn approval.
Not to stir up hatred toward pastors.
Not to encourage reckless accusations.
But to help someone discover what Scripture actually teaches.
One thoughtful share may reach a person who has been too frightened to ask for help.
Return to the Scriptures.
Read Hebrews 13, 1 Peter 5, Ezekiel 34, John 9, John 10, and Matthew 20 in their full contexts.
Do not build your convictions on one article, one pastor, or one isolated verse.
Examine the Word of God.
Seek wise counsel.
Learn to recognize the difference between Christ-centered leadership and spiritual domination.
Not because Gospel Warrior should replace your local church.
Not because any online ministry deserves unquestioning loyalty.
But because believers need daily encouragement to return to Scripture, examine their lives honestly, repent where necessary, and grow deeper in Jesus Christ.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, and even those who have lost confidence in organized religion to follow along.
Our desire is to point people toward the Savior, not toward dependence on a personality.
And for those who want to help us carry this mission further, there is another invitation.
It can help us continue, improve, and expand that work.
If this ministry has helped you, and you prayerfully believe supporting it is a wise use of what God has entrusted to you, your monthly contribution can be a meaningful expression of generosity.
You may choose to treat that support as part of your personal Christian giving, according to your convictions and the teaching of your church.
But please understand this clearly.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
That means your giving should be willing.
Not frightened.
Not manipulated.
Not extracted through guilt.
You can glorify Him through faithful obedience, love, generosity, prayer, service, and countless other acts of worship.
It helps sustain the labor behind the ministry and makes it possible to keep developing resources for others.
These free resources are part of our commitment to making biblical nourishment accessible.
It is an opportunity to help sustain and expand the work.
Keep reading His Word.
Keep testing what you hear against Scripture.
Keep praying for faithful pastors.
Keep supporting churches that genuinely shepherd God's people.
And never allow the failures of an abusive leader to convince you that Jesus is unworthy of your trust.
Because here is the truth I hope stays with you long after you've closed this article.
You can honor spiritual authority without surrendering your conscience.
You can love the Church without enabling abuse.
You can forgive without denying justice.
You can leave an unsafe congregation without leaving the Savior.
And you can begin again without pretending that what happened didn't hurt.
The Good Shepherd is not threatened by your desire for truth.
He is not offended when you seek safety from genuine harm.
He does not need manipulation to keep His people close.
His call is not, "Stay where you are being destroyed so a human leader can remain powerful."
His call is to follow Him.
And sometimes following Jesus means refusing to follow someone who has abandoned His example.
If you are still standing at that painful crossroads, afraid of what tomorrow will look like, remember the promise of Romans 8:38–39.
Neither death nor life, nor any other created thing, can separate those who belong to Christ from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
Not a pastor's anger.
Not a congregation's rejection.
Not the loss of a religious title.
Not the shame someone tried to place upon you.
Your hope is not held together by the approval of a spiritual leader.
Your hope is Jesus Christ.
So take the next faithful step.
Seek safety if you need it.
Seek truth.
Seek wise, trustworthy help.
Seek healthy Christian community.
And above all, seek the face of the One who gave His life for the sheep.
Because the man who made you afraid to leave was never the One who died to save you.
And when the shepherd who was supposed to protect you became the reason you were bleeding, the scars he left behind did not erase the name of the Savior who still calls you His own.
